analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prices for high-cost brand-name drugs and insulin, and caps seniors' drug costs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and expired in January 2023 with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Health Secretary to negotiate a maximum price for the most expensive brand-name drugs and all insulin products sold to Medicare, with an escalating tax on drug companies that refuse to negotiate. It would also cap annual and monthly out-of-pocket drug costs for Medicare beneficiaries, limit insulin cost-sharing in Medicare and employer and private plans, force companies to pay rebates when drug prices rise faster than inflation, and boost payment for biosimilar and vaccine coverage. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and anyone who relies on prescription drugs, especially insulin users, who would see negotiated maximum prices apply at the pharmacy counter, a cap on annual out-of-pocket drug spending, and inflation rebates when prices rise faster than the general price level.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a Drug Price Negotiation Program: starting in 2025, the Secretary picks the highest-spending single-source brand drugs (10 in 2025, rising to 20 by 2028) plus all insulin products and negotiates a 'maximum fair price' for Medicare, backed by a noncompliance excise tax that climbs from 65% to 95% of sales for manufacturers who refuse to sign an agreement [S3].

The negotiated price is capped at 75% of the non-federal average manufacturer price for shorter-monopoly drugs, 65% for drugs 12 to 16 years past approval, and 40% for drugs 16 or more years past approval — cutting prices most sharply for old, brand-name drugs that face no competition [S3].
It redesigns the Medicare Part D drug benefit and caps out-of-pocket spending, and imposes a monthly cap on cost-sharing in drug plans [S2].

It limits cost-sharing for insulin not just in Medicare Part D but also under employer plans (ERISA), the Public Health Service Act, and the tax code — so private and employer coverage would face insulin cost-sharing limits too [S3].
It requires manufacturers of Medicare Part B and Part D drugs to pay rebates when prices rise faster than inflation [S2].

It adds coverage of adult vaccines under Medicare Part D, expands vaccine access in Medicaid and CHIP, and temporarily boosts Medicare payment for biosimilar biological products to encourage lower-cost competition [S3].
It appropriates $300 million per year from fiscal 2022 through 2031 to run the negotiation program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose prices would be negotiated downward, whose older monopolies would face 40%-of-list price ceilings, who would owe inflation rebates, and who would face escalating excise taxes and civil money penalties for noncompliance. Federal taxpayers fund the $300 million annual program administration.

drawbacks.text: The program is narrow: only about 10 to 20 of the very highest-spending drugs are negotiated each year, and orphan drugs, low-spend drugs, and certain small biotech drugs are excluded from eligibility in the early years [S3].

Drugs only become eligible 7 years after approval (9 years before the negotiated price can apply) and biologics 11 years after licensure (13 years before the price applies), so manufacturers keep free pricing power through most of a drug's exclusivity period [S3].
Once negotiated, the maximum fair price only rises with the consumer price index in later years, so the benchmark does not track other market changes [S3].
The negotiated price determinations and drug selections are expressly not subject to administrative or judicial review, limiting manufacturers' and others' ability to challenge the process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries and insulin users the benefits are large and direct: a binding price ceiling at the point of sale, capped out-of-pocket spending, and protection against price spikes. The costs fall almost entirely on brand-name manufacturers' revenue rather than on consumers, and taxpayers pay $300 million a year to run the program. The main weakness is design, not balance: by excluding most drugs and waiting out the early monopoly years, the bill would leave the large majority of medicines outside the negotiated-price system. The bill also locks in the existing pharmacy-rebate system rather than eliminating it.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2022, it was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee, none of which ever acted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) introduced the Make Medicine Affordable Act on April 11, 2022 [S1].
The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — a split referral that means any one committee could let it sit [S5].
On April 12, 2022, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, which took no further action [S5].
No member from either party cosponsored the bill [S4].
No committee held a markup, no hearing is recorded in the action history, and no floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept un-negotiated Medicare prices and avoided the excise tax, inflation rebates, and cost-sharing caps the bill would have imposed. Medicare beneficiaries and insulin users did not get the lower prices and caps this bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so no partisan coalition formed around the bill one way or the other [S4].

industries.note: The bill would cut directly into their revenue through negotiated maximum prices, 40%-of-list ceilings on long-monopoly drugs, inflation rebates, and an excise tax reaching 95% of sales for noncompliance. Their interest in keeping prices un-negotiated runs against what the bill would do for patients and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug rebate intermediaries
industries.note: Title IV blocks implementation of the rule that would have eliminated the anti-kickback safe harbor for prescription drug rebates, keeping the existing rebate flow through PBMs in place. Rebates are negotiated behind closed doors and their full value does not always reach patients at the pharmacy counter.

industries.industry: Private Medicare drug plans (Part D and MA-PD)
industries.note: Plans would be required to cover every negotiated selected drug at no more than the maximum fair price and to submit pricing information. Their drug acquisition costs would fall alongside their members' cost-sharing.
Temporary higher Medicare payment for biosimilars is designed to pull cheaper competition into the market, which lowers costs for patients.
